name: In-silico labeling (ISL) pretraining for segmentation
what: Train a model to predict fluorescent labels (DAPI/CellMask) from label-free phase-contrast images, then use the predicted channels as pretraining supervision for segmentation, compared across training-set sizes.
why_better: Old plan derives supervision only from ~70 hand-drawn masks; ISL converts every co-acquired phase+fluorescence pair into dense pixel supervision, so segmentation quality per labeled image rises (paper: annotation requirement drops dramatically) - attacks the 70-image bottleneck of the Swin multi-task model directly, unlike Cellpose3 zero-shot pre-annotation which is an unpaired guess.
evidence: unverified (abstract: segmentation 'dramatically reduces' required annotations at smaller labeled sets; no numbers stated)
source_title: Learning with minimal effort: leveraging in silico labeling for cell and nucleus segmentation
fit_small_data: high - explicitly designed for low-annotation regimes; uses labeled + label-free pool exactly as available
fit_onnx_cpu: high - standard U-Net-style regressor, clean ONNX export
risk: Requires phase and fluorescence captured on the same field of view; if fluorescence exists for only a subset of fields, the paired set may be well under 70

name: IMPLICITSTAINER: deterministic non-GAN virtual staining via neural implicit functions
what: Reformulates image-to-image translation as a continuous per-pixel mapping (target pixel from source pixel embedding + local neighborhood + coordinates), giving deterministic, resolution-agnostic outputs without GAN or diffusion stochasticity.
why_better: GAN/diffusion ISL introduces stochasticity that causes hallucinations and structural distortion (paper's finding) and usually needs large datasets; the implicit mapping removes hallucination risk and is highlighted as robust in low-data regimes - beats the GAN route (already banned) and a plain pix2pix, claiming SOTA over >20 baselines, so it is the stronger non-GAN architecture for the ~70-pair setting.
evidence: unverified - 'SOTA performance across more than twenty baselines on virtual staining tasks (IHC and mIF)'; no numeric metric stated in abstract
source_title: IMPLICITSTAINER: Resolution Agnostic Data-Efficient Virtual Staining Using Neural Implicit Functions
fit_small_data: high - low-data regime robustness is a stated selling point
fit_onnx_cpu: medium - per-pixel implicit evaluation may be slow on CPU; CPU cost unverified, likely needs tiling
risk: Validated on histopathology, not 2D PC12 neurites; architecture is newer so ONNX porting may require custom ops

name: Downstream-task utility of virtual staining vs task-network capacity (caution)
what: Systematic study showing virtual staining's benefit for downstream segmentation/classification depends on the task network's capacity: with sufficiently large task networks, virtually-stained images do not improve - and can degrade - performance versus direct label-free input.
why_better: Gives a decision rule before spending ISL effort: if the final Swin multi-task model is large-capacity, feeding it phase contrast directly may be as good, and ISL effort is only worth it for the small student used in ONNX deployment - prevents wasting ~3-4 weeks building an ISL pipeline with zero downstream gain (old plan had no such check).
evidence: unverified (qualitative finding on biological datasets; no numbers in abstract)
source_title: On the Utility of Virtual Staining for Downstream Applications as it relates to Task Network Capacity
fit_small_data: high - exactly the small-data/small-model regime of this project
fit_onnx_cpu: high - an evaluation protocol, not a runtime model
risk: Findings from pathology/segmentation tasks; could understate benefits specific to thin 2-3 px neurites where synthetic contrast may genuinely help

name: btrack: Bayesian multi-object cell tracking
what: Mature Python tracker modeling cell position/velocity with Kalman-filter Bayesian inference to link detections across time-lapse frames; handles division, death, and missed detections; no learned components, actively maintained (335+ stars).
why_better: Old plan treats 0/6/24 h as independent conditions, so NTI is computed on population statistics with well-to-well and batch confounds; btrack links the same soma across the three time points with zero annotated tracks (the 70 masks contain no track labels), enabling per-cell longitudinal NTI and within-cell dose x time analysis.
evidence: unverified - repo description and docs only; no benchmark numbers seen in this search
source_title: btrack: Bayesian multi-object tracking (GitHub repository, btrack.readthedocs.io)
fit_small_data: high - requires no training data at all
fit_onnx_cpu: high - pure NumPy/Python, runs on any CPU offline
risk: 0/6/24 h sampling is very sparse for a Kalman motion model (it assumes motion continuity); PC12 soma drift over 24 h is small so it may still link, but must be validated on real trajectories

name: TrackASTRA: transformer-based cell tracking
what: Transformer that directly learns pairwise cell associations within a temporal window from annotated tracks, explicitly modeling dividing objects, and remains accurate with simple greedy linking (ECCV 2024).
why_better: Beats the manual per-dataset hyperparameter tuning that btrack/Ultrack linking requires by learning the association function; the 70 labeled fields can be extended to track annotations cheaply (soma centroids across 3 frames), and the learned associator should generalize across doses and time points without retuning.
evidence: unverified - abstract: 'on par with or better than highly tuned state-of-the-art cell tracking algorithms' on bacteria, cell cultures and fluorescent particles; no numbers
source_title: Trackastra: Transformer-based cell tracking for live-cell microscopy
fit_small_data: medium - needs track-pair annotations; feasible from 70 labeled fields but adds annotation cost, small scale may overfit
fit_onnx_cpu: medium - operates on sparse detection lists, not dense images, so CPU inference is cheap; ONNX export unverified
risk: Training data must come from our own dataset (no public PC12 phase-contrast tracks exist); few hours/conditions may be too little for the transformer to beat a tuned btrack

name: Ultrack: large-scale multi-hypotheses cell tracking via ultrametric contour maps
what: Computes tracks by selecting disjoint segments from a hierarchy of segmentation hypotheses while maximizing overlap between adjacent frames; state-of-the-art on the cell tracking challenge; accepts off-the-shelf segmentation models and ensembles of them.
why_better: The old plan already budgets a 5-seed ensemble for uncertainty; Ultrack converts that existing ensemble into a segmentation+tracking ensemble that improves both mask quality and track linking without any new labels - free lunch on top of the old plan's components.
evidence: unverified - abstract: 'state-of-the-art results in 3D images from the cell tracking challenge'; no numeric value given
source_title: Large-Scale Multi-Hypotheses Cell Tracking Using Ultrametric Contours Maps
fit_small_data: high - requires no 3D or track annotation; works with 2D segmentation hypotheses
fit_onnx_cpu: high - NumPy + integer linear programming (Gurobi/CBC), CPU-friendly
risk: ILP solve cost grows with instance count per well; Gurobi licensing for non-commercial use is fine, but a commercial desktop product would need the academic/community tier checked

name: GraphDINO: self-supervised GNN on neuron skeleton graphs
what: Self-supervised transformer representation learning for spatially embedded graphs (graph-specific augmentations, adapted positional encoding, AC-attention) that learns neuron morphology embeddings from unlabeled 3D morphologies.
why_better: Old plan feeds the NTI four hand-crafted parameters (length, branch count, angle, soma shape) plus a NETMORPH prior; GraphDINO learns morphology embeddings from our unlabelled pool (no labels needed for pretraining) and its clusterings are reported on par with expert feature-based classification - a data-driven morphology feature that should outperform hand-crafted NETMORPH descriptors at the NTI stage.
evidence: unverified - abstract: 'on par with manual feature-based classification by experts' and 'outperforms previous approaches on quantitative benchmarks predicting expert labels'; no numbers
source_title: Self-Supervised Graph Representation Learning for Neuronal Morphologies (GraphDINO)
fit_small_data: high - self-supervised, so only unlabeled skeleton graphs are needed; the 70 labeled cells suffice for the final NTI readout head
fit_onnx_cpu: medium - per-cell graphs are small (hundreds of nodes) so inference is trivial, but PyTorch-Geometric to ONNX export is fiddly; a pure-Python runtime is acceptable at this scale
risk: Pretraining data were 3D mouse cortical neurons; transfer to flat 2D PC12 phase-contrast skeletons is unproven; requires our skeleton graph extraction to be reliable first

name: TMD / persistence-image barcodes for toxicity morphometry
what: Topological Morphology Descriptor: a barcode of persistent intervals of the neuron tree, vectorized as persistence images; demonstrated to separate healthy from tauopathy neurons (diseased cells show shorter branches and fewer branches far from the soma), with 1-Wasserstein stability under tree perturbations; also yields 'topological morphology functions', Sholl-like curves recoverable from the barcode.
why_better: Replaces/augments the hand-crafted length/branch/angle features with a stability-proven topology code that is already shown to detect disease-like retraction - precisely the PC12 toxin response - so the NTI gains a descriptor whose robustness to skeletonization noise is guaranteed, whereas the old plan's raw NETMORPH descriptors have no such stability analysis (and automated Sholl is subsumed by the recoverable TMD functions).
evidence: unverified - significant healthy-vs-tauopathy difference and shorter/fewer-far branches reported; stability proven for 1-Wasserstein (companion paper); no single numeric metric in abstracts
source_title: Barcodes distinguish morphology of neuronal tauopathy
fit_small_data: high - no training; computed per cell from our own skeletons
fit_onnx_cpu: high - linear-cost spherical filtration + persistence computation in pure NumPy
risk: 2D PC12 skeletons are far smaller than 3D cortical neurons, so barcodes will have few intervals; discriminative power on toxin responses must be validated on the 70 labeled cells before being trusted in the NTI

name: CeNeuMorph: scale-adaptive self-supervised vision model for neurotoxicity morphometry
category: foundation models as frozen feature baseline
what: Self-supervised (scale-adaptive masked image modeling) vision model trained on a 27,117-image confocal benchmark of C. elegans dopaminergic neurons; fusing its visual features with morphological descriptors predicts dopamine-dependent behavioral deficits (R^2=0.498), and it was used to screen 180 agrochemicals, identifying a benzimidazole neurotoxicity moiety.
why_better: Externally validates the exact recipe this project needs - frozen vision features + morphology descriptors -> toxicity readout - and shows it beats generalist and biomedical foundation models on fine-lesion tasks (dendritic beading to soma shrinkage); a stronger frozen baseline than the old plan's 'basic DINOv2 mention', and a template for pretraining our own scale-adaptive MAE encoder on the unlabelled PC12 pool.
evidence: R^2=0.498 for dopamine-dependent behavioral deficit prediction; 27,117-image benchmark; 180-chemical screen (as stated in abstract)
source_title: A Scale-adaptive Vision Model Links C. elegans Neuronal Morphology to Behavior for Neurotoxicity Assessment
fit_small_data: medium - frozen encoder is ready to use; if we pretrain on our own pool, unlabelled fields are plentiful but 2D phase contrast is a domain gap from 3D confocal
fit_onnx_cpu: medium - ViT encoder inference on a batch of fields is CPU-feasible; ONNX export standard
risk: Domain gap (C. elegans confocal vs human PC12 phase contrast); model weights release unverified - if not public, only the recipe (scale-adaptive MAE) is transferable

name: Semi-supervised artifact/quality control for high-content screening
what: Evaluates self-supervised and transfer-learning encoders as base models for a few-shot detector of HCS image aberrations (out-of-focus blur, saturation, debris, auto-fluorescence, empty images).
why_better: Old plan has no QC gate, so bad fields (defocus, debris, evaporation edge) silently corrupt NTI statistics across wells; a small QC classifier on a transfer encoder (the paper finds transfer learning best and least hyperparameter-sensitive) flags untrustworthy images before NTI aggregation, using a few dozen flagged examples from our own pool.
evidence: unverified - transfer learning preferred over self-supervised for this task; no metric values stated
source_title: Comparison of semi-supervised learning methods for High Content Screening quality control
fit_small_data: high - semi-supervised/few-shot by design; tens of flagged examples suffice
fit_onnx_cpu: high - small CNN head, trivial on CPU
risk: Artifact taxonomy was defined for fluorescence HCS; phase-contrast failure modes (focus drift, edge evaporation, condensation) need our own label set

name: gSTA digital twin: IGA phase-field synthetic neurite deterioration + MetaFormer forecasting
what: High-throughput digital-twin framework: an isogeometric-analysis phase-field model generates diverse synthetic neurite deterioration patterns (retraction, atrophy, fragmentation), and a MetaFormer gated spatiotemporal attention network is trained on synthetic + experimental images to forecast future deterioration frames.
why_better: The mechanistic phase-field generator produces toxin-relevant pathology-specific training/augmentation samples - a direct upgrade over the old plan's rigid copy-paste augmentation (which moves intact cells, never simulating retraction/fragmentation) - and the forecaster can interpolate or replace the 24 h time point, reducing imaging load; average error 6.03% on experimental deterioration.
evidence: average error 1.9641% (synthetic) and 6.0339% (experimental) neurite deterioration (as stated in abstract)
source_title: High-throughput digital twin framework for predicting neurite deterioration using MetaFormer attention
fit_small_data: medium - synthetic data mitigates label scarcity; ML model trained on simulations plus few experimental images
fit_onnx_cpu: medium - MetaFormer attention over frame stacks; CPU-feasible but unverified
risk: Domain gap (iPSC-derived/mouse neurites vs 2D PC12 phase contrast); running the IGA phase-field simulator needs dedicated tooling and tuning to match PC12 morphology

name: ALMAB-DC: active learning + multi-armed bandits for sequential dose-response experiment design
what: Gaussian-process surrogate with uncertainty-aware acquisition, a UCB/Thompson-sampling bandit controller allocating evaluations across parallel workers, and an asynchronous scheduler, for expensive gradient-free dose-response experimentation.
why_better: The old plan's fixed 7-dose x 3-time grid wastes wells on redundant conditions; ALMAB-DC selects the next most informative (dose, time) from predicted NTI uncertainty and achieves lower simple regret than Equal Spacing, Random and D-optimal designs on dose-response tasks - turning the follow-up campaigns into uncertainty-driven design instead of static grids.
evidence: lower simple regret than Equal Spacing, Random, and D-optimal designs on dose-response optimization (as stated in abstract; no numeric values)
source_title: ALMAB-DC: Active Learning, Multi-Armed Bandits, and Distributed Computing for Sequential Experimental Design and Black-Box Optimization
fit_small_data: high - designed for tight evaluation budgets; our 21-condition grid + follow-ups are exactly the regime
fit_onnx_cpu: high - GP + bandit, no neural network; the NTI surrogate can be the old plan's small NN
risk: The primary 7x3 screen may be a funder protocol requirement; sequential design applies to follow-up campaigns, and the GP surrogate needs a well-calibrated NTI uncertainty (the old plan's temperature scaling helps)

name: StrokeSeg2: knowledge distillation + ONNX FP16 for compact desktop segmentation apps
what: Cross-platform C++/Qt application that adapts an nnU-Net-class segmentation pipeline into a portable offline desktop product via knowledge distillation to a small student model plus ONNX Runtime inference with FP16 quantization, shipped as a self-contained installer.
why_better: Proven recipe for the old plan's 'ONNX Runtime on CPU' desktop app: distillation was the primary efficiency driver (>90% energy reduction, 84% average inference-time reduction) with a 0.84M-parameter / 2.1 MB student - a concrete blueprint for packaging the Swin/U-Net heads as an offline Windows desktop instead of a heavy Python environment.
evidence: >90% energy reduction, 84% average inference-time reduction; 0.84M-parameter student at 2.1 MB disk footprint (as stated in abstract)
source_title: StrokeSeg2: Stroke Lesion Segmentation in Clinical Research Workflows
fit_small_data: high - distillation uses teacher predictions, no additional labels needed
fit_onnx_cpu: high - ONNX Runtime FP16 demonstrated on CPU, iGPU and dedicated GPU
risk: Distilling the multi-task Swin outputs (soma instance + neurite semantic + skeleton) is trickier than single masks; FP16 precision loss on 2-3 px thin neurites must be verified against the neurite Dice >= 0.80 target

name: OpenVINO as CPU execution backend (runtime benchmark)
what: Systematic comparison of PyTorch, ONNX Runtime, OpenVINO and TensorRT for machine-vision inference (CNN and transformer-based vision models) across CPU and GPU platforms.
why_better: Directly challenges the old plan's 'ONNX Runtime on CPU' choice: on the tested hardware, OpenVINO achieved the lowest CPU inference time of all four frameworks - a drop-in runtime swap (Intel CPU desktops are common) that speeds up per-field inference without touching model weights.
evidence: unverified - abstract states OpenVINO lowest CPU inference time and TensorRT lowest GPU time; no speedup factor given
source_title: Benchmarking Edge Inference Strategies for Deep Learning Models in Industrial Machine Vision
risk: Operator-coverage gaps for custom ops; post-hoc skeletonization and clDice-style processing stay outside the graph; must verify parity on our exact models and the target Windows machines
